title: Cellar and Smile
premise: Ada Yarrow returns to the family farmhouse to bury their twin brother, Wren, only to find that everyone in town—including the funeral director—insists it was Ada who died twelve years ago. On the porch sits Tam, Ada's childhood imaginary friend, unchanged after two decades, who claims he was invited in long ago and has been keeping the house—and something beneath the cellar—fed ever since. As the night unravels, Ada discovers that 'Wren' buried in the casket is a stranger, that the real Wren may have taken Ada's place years ago to escape a bargain, and that the thing in the cellar collects identities like debts. To survive until sunrise, Ada must decide whether to pay the inherited debt with their own name or break the cycle by giving the thing nothing at all—not even recognition—ending the Yarrow curse by walking out of the house as no one at all.
about_author: Mirabel Eriksen is the pen name of a former rural archivist who spent years cataloguing estate records and unclaimed inheritances across the upper Midwest. Their fiction blends bureaucratic dread with folk horror, exploring how families pass down more than property.

chapters.title: The Wrong Twin
chapters.summary: Ada arrives at the farmhouse for the funeral, POV Ada, third-person limited. The funeral director greets them with condolences for their own death, showing a headstone with Ada's name dated twelve years ago. The emotional beat is disorientation—the first crack in Ada's certainty about which twin survived.

chapters.title: Porch Light
chapters.summary: Ada settles into the house for the night before the burial. On the porch sits Tam, the imaginary friend, exactly as remembered at age eight. He says he's been waiting and that the house needs feeding tonight. POV Ada; the beat shifts from grief to creeping recognition that childhood fears were real.

chapters.title: Inventory of Noises
chapters.summary: Ada catalogs twelve years of explained-away sounds: footsteps above empty rooms, the cellar door found open. Tam narrates alongside, correcting each explanation with what actually happened. POV alternates between Ada's present and flashbacks. The beat is the horror of realizing one's whole adult life was built on denial.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Tam explains the family bargain: generations of Yarrows traded a name to the thing below for prosperity, and children 'invite' it unknowingly through games. Ada remembers the tea party, the promise made. POV Ada with Tam's voice intruding. The beat is guilt—the invitation was Ada's.

chapters.title: The Casket Question
chapters.summary: Unable to sleep, Ada drives to the funeral home and views the body: an unknown man wearing Wren's ring. The director, Mrs. Okafor, quietly reveals she's seen this before with the Yarrows and warns Ada not to open the cellar. POV Ada; beat is dread hardening into resolve.

chapters.title: Wren's Room, Sealed
chapters.summary: Ada breaks into Wren's locked bedroom and finds journals in Ada's own handwriting, dated after the supposed death—evidence Wren lived as Ada for years, or that names were swapped long ago. Tam grows agitated, begging Ada to stop reading. POV Ada; beat is identity dissolving—Ada cannot prove who they are.

chapters.title: Neighbors Who Remember Differently
chapters.summary: A surviving neighbor, old Halvorsen, tells Ada that on the night twelve years ago, both twins went down to the cellar and only one came up—but which one, even he won't say. The thing below has begun climbing the stairs early. POV Ada; beat is isolation, the last outside witness refusing clarity.

chapters.title: Descending
chapters.summary: With sunrise hours away and the house sealing itself, Ada opens the cellar door deliberately. Below: a room of mirrors and ledgers listing every Yarrow name, each crossed out except one line where 'Ada' and 'Wren' share a single entry. POV Ada; beat is terrible clarity—the twins were always one debt split in two.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: Climax. The thing offers Ada a choice: reclaim the name and live, but feed it forever through future children, or surrender both names and let the line end. Tam reveals he is the previous generation's surrendered child, kept as bait. Ada refuses the trade and speaks no name at all. POV Ada; beat is sacrifice without heroics.

chapters.title: No One at All
chapters.summary: Resolution. Dawn comes; the house stands ordinary and empty. Ada walks out unnamed—no records match them, the funeral proceeds for a stranger, and the ledger's last line fades. Free but erased, Ada begins again elsewhere, occasionally feeling watched by nothing at all. POV Ada; beat is bittersweet liberation: justice achieved by refusing inheritance entirely.
